'''Barry James Thompson''' (born 1978) is an Australian and British [[Developmental biology|developmental biologist]] and [[Cancer|cancer biologist]]. Thompson is known for identifying genes, proteins and mechanisms involved in [[epithelial polarity]], [[morphogenesis]] and [[cell signaling]] via the [[Wnt signaling pathway|Wnt]] and [[Hippo signaling pathway]]s, which have key roles in human [[cancer]].

==Early life and education==
Barry Thompson was born in 1978 into a British-Australian family. He was raised on the [[Atherton Tableland]] and in [[Brisbane]] in the state of [[Queensland]] (Australia).  He attended [[Atherton, Queensland|Atherton]] State Primary School and [[Brisbane State High School]] and graduated as school Dux in 1995.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://brisbaneshs.eq.edu.au/ourschool/History/Pages/Past-Dux-of-school.aspx|title = Past Dux of School|date = 21 November 2019}}</ref>

==Scientific career==
Thompson became interested in [[developmental biology]] and the control of tissue [[growth hormone|growth]] in 2000 when studying BSc(Hons) at the [[University of Queensland]]'s Institute for Molecular Biology (IMB) with Professor Michael Waters.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Identification of genes induced by growth hormone in rat liver using cDNA arrays|last1=Thompson|first1=Barry|last2=Shang|first2=Catherine|last3=Waters|first3=Michael|volume=141|issue=11|pages = 4321–4324|year=2000|journal=[[Endocrinology]]|doi=10.1210/endo.141.11.7874|pmid = 11089569|doi-access=free}}</ref>

He earned his PhD degree at the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology]] and [[University of Cambridge]] (United Kingdom), where he studied the [[Wnt signaling pathway]] in [[Drosophila melanogaster]] with Dr Mariann Bienz.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A new nuclear component of the Wnt signalling pathway|journal=[[Nature Cell Biology]]|last1=Thompson|first1=Barry|last2=Townsley|first2=Fiona|last3=Rosin|first3=Rina|last4=Musisi|first4=Hannah|last5=Bienz|first5=Mariann|s2cid=23942463|year=2002|volume=4|issue=5|pages=367–73|doi=10.1038/ncb786|pmid=11988739}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=A Complex of Armadillo, Legless, and Pygopus Coactivates dTCF to Activate Wingless Target Genes|journal=[[Current Biology]]|last1=Thompson|first1=Barry|s2cid=6121751|year=2004|volume=14|issue=6|pages=1–20|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2004.02.026|pmid=15043810|doi-access=free|bibcode=2004CBio...14..458T }}</ref>

He then moved to Germany to work at the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] with Prof Stephen M Cohen. There he studied the role of the [[Hippo signaling pathway]] during Drosophila development.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Hippo pathway regulates the ''bantam'' microRNA to control cell proliferation and apoptosis in Drosophila|journal=[[Cell (journal)|Cell]]|last1=Thompson|first1=B.|last2=Cohen|first2=S.M.|s2cid=15264514|year=2006|volume=126|issue=4|pages=767–74|pmid=16923395|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2006.07.013|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2007, Thompson was a visiting scientist at the [[Research Institute of Molecular Pathology]] in [[Vienna]] (Austria), where he worked in the laboratory of Dr [[Barry Dickson]] to perform a genome-wide in vivo RNAi screen in Drosophila.  In 2008, Thompson established his own laboratory at the [[Cancer Research UK]] [[London Research Institute]], which became part of the [[Francis Crick Institute]] in 2015.  In 2019, Thompson was appointed Professor at the [[John Curtin School of Medical Research]] at the [[Australian National University]]. His service was terminated in October 2023 due to his actions of sexual harassment.<ref>{{Cite web |last=DeadestLift |date=2022-05-15 |title=Heads up for women who shop at Dickson - harassment and unwanted attention |url=http://www.reddit.com/r/canberra/comments/upy7xg/heads_up_for_women_who_shop_at_dickson_harassment/ |access-date=2024-05-22 |website=r/canberra}}</ref>

==Research areas==
===Epithelial cell polarity===
His laboratory works on the molecular mechanisms of [[epithelial polarity]], including both apical-basal polarity and planar cell polarity, using [[Drosophila melanogaster]] epithelial tissues as an experimental model system.  His laboratory discovered that apical-basal polarisation of the transmembrane protein [[CRB1|Crumbs]] - a key apical determinant - depends upon both a [[Cdc42]]-driven positive feedback loop as well as mutual antagonism between apical and basolateral determinants.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Positive feedback and mutual antagonism combine to polarize Crumbs in the Drosophila follicle cell epithelium|last1=Fletcher|first1=G.C.|last2=Lucas|first2=E.P.|last3=Brain|first3=R.|last4=Tournier|first4=A.|last5=Thompson|first5=B.J.|s2cid=16648144|journal=[[Current Biology]]|year=2012|volume=22|issue=12|pages=1116–1122|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2012.04.020|pmid=22658591|doi-access=free|bibcode=2012CBio...22.1116F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Cell polarity: models and mechanisms from yeast, worms and flies|last=Thompson|first=B.J.|s2cid=7117523|journal=[[Development (journal)|Development]]|year=2013|volume=140|issue=1|pages=13–21|doi=10.1242/dev.083634|pmid=23222437|doi-access=free}}</ref> The Cdc42-driven positive feedback loop involves recruitment of [[Cdc42]] complexes by Crumbs, followed by [[Cdc42]]-mediated polarisation of the cytoskeleton, including both [[actin]] filaments and [[microtubules]], that allow transport of Crumbs-containing vesicles by the microtubule motor protein [[Dynein]] and the actin motor protein [[MYO5A|Myosin-V]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Shot and Patronin polarise microtubules to direct membrane traffic and biogenesis of microvilli in epithelia|last1=Khanal|first1=I.|last2=Elbediwy|first2=A.|last3=Diaz de la Loza|first3=M.C.|last4=Fletcher|first4=G.C.|last5=Thompson|first5=B.J.|journal=[[Journal of Cell Science]]|year=2016|volume=129|issue=13|pages=2651–2659|doi=10.1242/jcs.189076|pmid=27231092|pmc=4958304}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=The cytoskeletal motor proteins Dynein and MyoV direct apical transport of Crumbs.|last1=Aguilar-Aragon|first1=M.|last2=Fletcher|first2=G.|last3=Thompson|first3=B.J.|journal=[[Developmental Biology]]|year=2020|volume=459|issue=2|pages=126–137|doi=10.1016/j.ydbio.2019.12.009|pmid=31881198|pmc=7090908}}</ref> How [[Cdc42]] polarises the cytoskeleton remains an important unsolved problem, but [[Cdc42]] appears to act primarily via activating the kinases aPKC and Pak1 in Drosophila follicle cells.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Pak1 Kinase Maintains Apical Membrane Identity in Epithelia|last1=Aguilar-Aragon|first1=M.|last2=Elbediwy|first2=A.|last3=Foglizzo|first3=V.|last4=Fletcher|first4=G.C.|last5=Li|first5=V.S.W|last6=Thompson|first6=B.J.|journal=[[Cell Reports]]|year=2018|volume=22|issue=7|pages=1639–1646|doi=10.1016/j.celrep.2018.01.060|pmid=29444419|pmc=5847184}}</ref>

His laboratory also discovered that planar cell polarisation of the atypical [[myosin]] Dachs by the Fat and Dachsous [[cadherins]] is responsible for polarising tension at [[adherens junctions]] and thus influencing the orientation of cell shapes and cell divisions within the plane of the epithelium.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Planar polarization of the atypical myosin Dachs orients cell divisions in Drosophila|last1=Mao|first1=Y.|last2=Tournier|first2=A.|last3=Bates|first3=P.|last4=Gale|first4=J.E.|last5=Tapon|first5=N.|last6=Thompson|first6=B.J.|journal=[[Genes & Development]]|year=2011|volume=25|issue=2|pages=131–136|doi=10.1101/gad.610511|pmid=21245166|pmc=3022259}}</ref> His lab subsequently found that this involved recruitment of the ubiquitin ligase FbxL7 to Fat, in order to degrade Dachs on one side of the cell, such that Dachs binds to Dachsous on the opposite side of the cell.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The ubiquitin ligase FbxL7 regulates the Dachsous-Fat-Dachs system in Drosophila|last1=Rodrigues-Campos|first1=M.|last2=Thompson|first2=B.J.|journal=[[Development (journal)|Development]]|year=2014|volume=141|issue=21|pages=4098–4103|doi=10.1242/dev.113498|pmid=25256343|pmc=4302899}}</ref>

===Epithelial cell division and spindle orientation===
Thompson's laboratory found that cell divisions in epithelia can also be oriented by mechanical forces arising from adjacent tissues growing at different rates.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Differential proliferation rates generate patterns of mechanical tension that orient tissue growth|last1=Mao|first1=Y.|last2=Tournier|first2=A.|last3=Hoppe|first3=A.|last4=Kester|first4=L.|last5=Thompson|first5=B.J.|last6=Tapon|first6=N.|journal=[[EMBO Journal]]|year=2013|volume=32|issue=21|pages=2790–2803|doi=10.1038/emboj.2013.197|pmid=24022370|pmc=3817460}}</ref> In order for the [[mitotic spindle]] to orient in response to planar forces, highly columnar pseudostratified epithelial cells must round up at [[mitosis]] in a process that involves the [[Aurora A]] and B kinases, activation of Rho-mediated actomyosin contractility, remodelling of [[adherens junctions]], and removal of the Lgl protein from the plasma membrane to allow spindle orienting factors to interact with Dlg/Scrib proteins and thereby align the spindle within the plane of the epithelium.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Aurora kinases phosphorylate Lgl to induce mitotic spindle orientation in Drosophila epithelia|last1=Bell|first1=G.P.|last2=Fletcher|first2=G.C.|last3=Brain|first3=R.|last4=Thompson|first4=B.J|journal=[[Current Biology]]|year=2015|volume=25|issue=1|pages=61–68|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2014.10.052|pmid=25484300|pmc=4291145|bibcode=2015CBio...25...61B }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Adherens junction remodeling during mitotic rounding of pseudostratified epithelial cells|last1=Aguilar-Aragon|first1=M.|last2=Bonello|first2=T.T.|last3=Bell|first3=G.P.|last4=Fletcher|first4=G.C|last5=Thompson|first5=B.J.|s2cid=13953651|journal=[[Current Biology]]|year=2015|volume=25|issue=1|pages=61–68|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2014.10.052|pmid=25484300|pmc=4291145|doi-access=free|bibcode=2015CBio...25...61B }}</ref>

===Epithelial morphogenesis===
While epithelial [[cell polarity]] and [[cell proliferation]] are fundamental to the construction of an epithelium, and can influence the form of the entire tissue, epithelial morphogenesis also depends fundamentally on anchorage to the [[extracellular matrix]] (ECM). Thompson's lab showed that synthesis and enzymatic remodelling of the ECM were crucial to the shaping of [[Drosophila melanogaster]] tissues, particularly for formation of the adult fly wings, legs and halteres during [[metamorphosis]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Patterned Anchorage to the Apical Extracellular Matrix Defines Tissue Shape in the Developing Appendages of Drosophila|last1=Ray|first1=R.P.|last2=Matamoro-Vidal|first2=A.|last3=Ribeiro|first3=P.S.|last4=Tapon|first4=N|last5=Houle|first5=D.|last6=Salaar-Cuidad|first6=I.|last7=Thompson|first7=B.J.|journal=[[Developmental Cell]]|year=2015|volume=34|issue=3|pages=310–22|doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2015.06.019|pmid=26190146|pmc=4539345}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Apical and Basal Matrix Remodeling Control Epithelial Morphogenesis|last1=Diaz de la Loza|first1=M.D.|last2=Ray|first2=R.P.|last3=Ganguly|first3=P.S.|last4=Alt|first4=S.|last5=Davis|first5=J.R.|last6=Hoppe|first6=A.|last7=Tapon|first7=N.|last8=Thompson|first8=B.J.|journal=[[Developmental Cell]]|year=2018|volume=46|issue=1|pages=23–39|doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2018.06.006|pmid=29974861|pmc=6035286}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Control of tissue morphogenesis by the HOX gene Ultrabithorax|last1=Diaz de la Loza|first1=M.D.|last2=Loker|first2=R.|last3=Mann|first3=R.S.|last4=Thompson|first4=B.J.|s2cid=49656207|journal=[[Development (journal)|Development]]|year=2020|volume=147|issue=5|pages=23–39|doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2018.06.006|pmid=29974861|pmc=6035286|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Hippo signaling===
Thompson's lab discovered several components of the [[Hippo signaling pathway]] in Drosophila melanogaster (including Kibra,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Kibra is a regulator of the Salvador/Warts/Hippo signaling network|last1=Genevet|first1=A.|last2=Wehr|first2=M.C.|last3=Brain|first3=R.|last4=Thompson|first4=B.J.|last5=Tapon|first5=N.|journal=[[Developmental Cell]]|year=2010|volume=18|issue=2|pages=300–308|doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2009.12.011|pmid=20159599|pmc=2845807}}</ref> Spectrins,<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Spectrin cytoskeleton regulates the Hippo signalling pathway|last1=Fletcher|first1=G.C.|last2=Elbediwy|first2=A.|last3=Khanal|first3=I.|last4=Ribeiro|first4=P.S.|last5=Tapon|first5=N.|last6=Thompson|first6=B.J.|s2cid=25838419|journal=[[Developmental Cell]]|year=2010|volume=18|issue=2|pages=300–308|doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2009.12.011|pmid=20159599|pmc=2845807|doi-access=free}}</ref> Mask<ref>{{cite journal|title=Mask proteins are cofactors of Yorkie/YAP in the Hippo pathway.|last1=Sidor|first1=C.M.|last2=Brain|first2=R.|last3=Thompson|first3=B.J.|s2cid=16722199|journal=[[Current Biology]]|year=2013|volume=23|issue=3|pages=223–228|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2012.11.061|pmid=23333315|doi-access=free|bibcode=2013CBio...23..223S }}</ref>) and that this pathway functions to sense mechanical strain during development of epithelial cells in vivo,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Mechanical strain regulates the Hippo pathway in Drosophila|last1=Fletcher|first1=G.C.|last2=Diaz-de-la-Loza|first2=M.D.|last3=Borreguero-Munoz|first3=N.|last4=Holder|first4=M.|last5=Aguilar-Aragon|first5=M.|last6=Thompson|first6=B.J.|journal=[[Development (journal)|Development]]|year=2018|volume=145|issue=5|pages=dev159467|doi=10.1242/dev.159467|pmid=29440303|pmc=5868995}}</ref> as well as to sense nutritional status via the hormonal [[Insulin]]/[[Insulin-like growth factor 1|IGF-1]] and [[Phosphoinositide 3-kinase|PI3K]]-[[Protein kinase B|Akt]] pathway,<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Hippo pathway integrates PI3K-Akt signals with mechanical and polarity cues to control tissue growth|last1=Borreguero-Munoz|first1=N.|last2=Fletcher|first2=G.C.|last3=Aguilar-Aragon|first3=M.|last4=Elbediwy|first4=A.|last5=Vincent-Mistiaen|first5=Z.I.|last6=Thompson|first6=B.J.|journal=[[PLOS Biology]]|year=2019|volume=17|issue=10|article-number=e3000509|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.3000509|pmid=31613895|pmc=6814241 |doi-access=free }}</ref> in order to control cell proliferation, cellular morphology, and invasive cell migration. His lab has also had a major interest in the role of the Hippo pathway in mammals, including humans, where (unlike Drosophila) the pathway also responds to input from [[Integrin]]-[[Src family kinase]] signals to enable the mechanical control of epithelial cell proliferation and tissue regeneration,  .<ref>{{cite journal|title=Integrin signalling regulates YAP and TAZ to control skin homeostasis.|last1=Elbwediwy|first1=A.|last2=Vincent-Mistiaen|first2=Z.I.|last3=et|first3=al|last4=Thompson|first4=B.J.|journal=[[Development (journal)|Development]]|year=2016|volume=143|issue=10|pages=1674–1687|doi=10.1242/dev.133728|pmid=26989177|pmc=4874484}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Evolution of mechanotransduction via YAP/TAZ in animal epithelia.|last1=Elbediwy|first1=A.|last2=Thompson|first2=B.J.|journal=[[Current Opinion in Cell Biology]]|year=2018|volume=51|pages=117–123|doi=10.1016/j.ceb.2018.02.003|pmid=29477107|doi-access=free}}</ref>
